title: Evolution of Concepts in Language Model Pre-Training
claim: One shared sparse dictionary decomposes activations from many training snapshots, so each feature's evolution can be tracked and interpreted.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, stacked snapshot cards feeding a feature bar with histograms
description: The left half, titled 'Collecting Activations', shows a stack of overlapping translucent cards labeled Snapshot 0 to Snapshot 5. The cards shift from grey to deeper blue, with a 'Training Progress' arrow above them. Each card holds Layer i and Layer i+1 boxes and a small row of activation squares. A single input sentence, 'The fox jumps over the lazy dog', feeds all snapshots from below through bracket arrows. Blue and orange curved arrows run from every snapshot into the right half, a wide blue bar of circles that stand for crosscoder features. Two of the circles are highlighted. Each highlighted circle links to a histogram of decoder norms across snapshots: a blue one for 'Form at initialization' and an orange one for 'Emerge at mid-training'. Below each histogram is a text panel of top-activating examples, 'Jump' Feature and Singular Verb, with the key words highlighted in orange. The headings 'Decoder Norms' and 'Interpretation' label the right side.
caption: Overview of our method. The crosscoder is trained to decompose activations of multiple pre-training snapshots (left) into sparse features (right).
abstract: Language models obtain extensive capabilities through pre-training. However, the pre-training process remains a black box. In this work, we track linear interpretable feature evolution across pre-training snapshots using a sparse dictionary learning method called crosscoders. We find that most features begin to form around a specific point, while more complex patterns emerge in later training stages. Feature attribution analyses reveal causal connections between feature evolution and downstream performance. Our feature-level observations are highly consistent with previous findings on Transformer's two-stage learning process, which we term a statistical learning phase and a feature learning phase. Our work opens up the possibility to track fine-grained representation progress during language model learning dynamics.
